I will be brief. First, I would like to thank Italy and Croatia for hosting this meeting. The situation before us is dire. The fragility of our global food system has never been so obvious. Immediate impact was already perceived in the wake of the food crisis precipitated by Russia's aggression against Ukraine, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and more recently, the disruptions of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. And more will come with the incoming super El Nino. The humanitarian data is alarming. WFP is clear. 45 million additional people could fall into acute food insecurity. And the longer it lasts, the worse it will be. This is the reason why France, as G7 presidency, established a working group dedicated to fertilizers. It has since worked on a roadmap to address the supply disruption and threaten the resilience of food systems. This roadmap seeks to address emergency, but also to foster resilience of our food systems. In the short term, this framework aims to facilitate the delivery of food aid by reducing logistical costs and rerouting food. We must mobilize and relocate funding from international and regional financial institutions to ensure access for vulnerable countries to food and fertilizer markets. In the medium and long term, we will accelerate this transition by strengthening anticipation capacities, enhancing coordination, and pushing for greater diversification of food and fertilizer supply sources. We must conceive of an agricultural future less dependent on imported inputs, more adaptable and sustainable, and capable of nourishing the entirety of the world's population. The imperative before us extends beyond a mere response to present crisis. It is to establish the resilience of our populations as an absolute and shared priority. I thank you.

Thank you. And thank you for invitation for Latvia to participate. To be clear, all economies across the globe are affected by attacks and threats on freedom of navigation, be it in Hormuz, the Red Sea, or Black Sea. However, it is the most vulnerable, least well-off parts of our global community across Africa, South Asia, and humanitarian regions, especially in active conflict zones and humanitarian emergencies that feel the effects the hardest. The supply chain disruptions, rising fuel prices, food prices, shortage of fertilizers mean that millions more are facing acute food insecurity as the harvest season continues to be severely affected and consequences will last even if freedom of navigation is restored. Other attempts by state actors to either sidestep or deliberately breach international law are additional risk multipliers. endangering maritime trade, communications, and environment. Among these threats, we must include the shadow fleet operating outside any safety parameters to unlawfully evade sanctions. Another key risk stems from sabotage against the subsea cable infrastructure worldwide. A robust and meaningful response to these complex challenges involves a multilayered effort. First, we must redouble on our commitment and strengthen the implementation of international law at sea, as reflected in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. International waterways are governed by clear legal principles, and no political considerations may interfere with freedom of navigation. Another layer is increased awareness, raising and coordination at all levels, most notably within the IMO, but also in regional organizations and other fora, while keeping the Council seized on threats that undermine navigational rights and freedoms. Allow me to conclude by reiterating our call for an immediate cessation of attacks against lawful civilian shipping, including in and around the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, and against the Ukrainian grain export infrastructure in the Black Sea. Latvia will remain a steadfast defender of maritime security and free and safe navigation. Thank you.
